howtos.title: Run agents from one home repo
howtos.what: Matt Pocock's pattern: one repo holds skills, steering files and wiki, and points the agent at your other repos.
copy: Create one 'Home Repo' that holds your skills, steering files and wiki.
Run the agent from inside the Home Repo.
In its AGENTS.md, point to local clones of your other repos.
Use it to make sweeping changes across multiple repos from one place.
howtos.whenToUse: When agent tooling is scattered across several repos or a change must span many codebases.

howtos.title: Give the coding agent ownership of the codebase
howtos.what: Anthropic's Fable 5.2 line that made the model merge repeated code in about half of tries, versus under a tenth without it.
copy: This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it.
howtos.whenToUse: When a coding agent is too cautious to improve or refactor existing code.

howtos.title: Plan with Fable 5.2, then build with Opus 5.5
howtos.what: A workflow to stretch limited Fable usage: use it only to plan and audit, then hand the plan to Opus to build.
copy: Use Fable only for planning and docs.
Have it audit the plan until it reaches highest confidence, with no clear gaps and no overengineering.
Make sure it writes out every step.
Hand the plan to Opus 5.5 to build.
howtos.whenToUse: When the premium model's usage limits run out faster than your build work.

howtos.title: Reset your agent setup at every major model drop
howtos.what: A two-step checklist so old instructions don't hold a new model back.
copy: Always read the model card.
Consider removing your existing skills and AGENTS.md files.
howtos.whenToUse: Right after a major model release, before you keep using your old agent setup.

howtos.title: Audit every project when a new model ships
howtos.what: One prompt that has a coding agent find broken, inconsistent, inefficient or unneeded code, fix the sure things and list the rest.
copy: Read this entire project and find everything that’s broken, inconsistent, inefficient, or no longer needed. Fix what you’re sure about and list the rest for me to review.
howtos.whenToUse: Right after a new model release, run it on each project you own.

howtos.title: Explain the why, not the what, to your AI
howtos.what: In AI grilling sessions, describe the user problem instead of the feature you want built.
copy: State the problem, not the feature.
Bad: "I want to build an analytics panel for admins with graphs and filters".
Good: "Admins can't currently see an overview of the important data in the app".
howtos.whenToUse: When starting a planning or grilling session with a coding agent on a new feature.

howtos.title: Hide the bulk of AI-written PR descriptions behind a fold
howtos.what: Wrap most of an AI-generated GitHub PR description in a collapsed <details><summary> block so reviewers see less slop.
copy: Put the bulk of the AI-generated PR description inside a <details><summary> HTML block, which GitHub Markdown renders collapsed.
howtos.whenToUse: When coding agents write long PR descriptions that tire out human reviewers.

howtos.title: Have an agent tune the slower version until it beats the faster one
howtos.what: After an agent builds the same function two ways, ask it to rewrite the slower one to match or beat the faster.
copy: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation
howtos.whenToUse: When an agent has built and benchmarked two implementations and one lags on speed.

howtos.title: Build an iOS app from rivals' worst reviews with agents
howtos.what: Steps to find a weak, high-revenue utility app, mine its 1-2 star reviews with an agent, and build a better one.
copy: Pick low-rated, high-revenue utility apps.
Use facundoolano/app-store-scraper to pull every review for the top 20.
Have an agent cluster the 1 and 2 star reviews into the top 5 complaints and quote the users.
Put the top 5 complaints in a skill.
Build with Claude Code plus Apple's Xcode plugin, cameroncooke/XcodeBuildMCP and joshuayoes/ios-simulator-mcp.
Use Apple Foundation Models for on-device inference.
Test with Maestro.
howtos.whenToUse: When you want to pick and build an iOS app idea grounded in real user complaints.

howtos.title: Make your coding agent list files before opening any
howtos.what: A prompt that has the agent name and justify the files it needs, wait for approval, then make the smallest fix.
copy: Before opening any files, list the exact files you need for this task and why. Check the file tree or search to find them, but don't open anything else. If you need more, stop and ask me first. Then, after I approve the list, make the smallest, highest-confidence change that fully solves our problem.
howtos.whenToUse: When an agent over-reads a large codebase and you want tighter context and smaller changes.

howtos.title: Audit bank CSVs with a Claude CFO prompt
howtos.what: Export 12 months of bank CSVs and have Claude find cuts, keeps, and renegotiations without account access.
copy: Be my CFO. Find every place I lose money, biggest first. Remove transfers between my own accounts so nothing counts twice. List every recurring charge, with its price and next renewal. Ask me 5 to 10 questions before you give advice. Then tell me what to CUT, KEEP, or RENEGOTIATE, with yearly savings. Use code for every number. Never ask for a password or account number.
howtos.whenToUse: When you want a spend audit from local bank CSVs without giving Claude account logins.

howtos.title: Re-run skill evals on each new model and delete what it outgrew
howtos.what: Use eval loops on your agent skills so each model upgrade shows which skills you can remove.
copy: Run eval-driven development loops on your agent skills.
When a new model ships, compare it with and without each skill.
Remove skills the model no longer needs, as Garry did with /investigate after Opus 5.5.
howtos.whenToUse: After a model upgrade, when your agent carries custom skills that may now slow it down.

howtos.title: Add a thorough-and-bold prompt suffix
howtos.what: Append one line that pushes deeper analysis and stronger recommendations on any model reply.
copy: Be thorough in your analysis and bold in your recommendations
howtos.whenToUse: When a model hedges or stays shallow and you want sharper, more decisive output.

howtos.title: Spend inference on deterministic outcomes
howtos.what: Drive agent loops by hand and use tokens to create outcomes that do not depend on model quirks, so better models lift you automatically.
copy: Drive your agent loops by hand instead of buying a software-factory product.
Spend inference where you can create deterministic outcomes that do not rely on model behavior.
Prefer good software engineering and token-efficient paths over marketing categories.
As the model improves, those deterministic paths uplift automatically without a factory rewrite.
howtos.whenToUse: When a vendor pitch for an agent software factory competes with simply spending more inference on well-engineered loops.

howtos.title: Run LangChain subagents in the background
howtos.what: Make a Deep Agents subagent async so the orchestrator stays responsive while long work runs in the background.
copy: In Managed Deep Agents, set "async": True on the subagent definition (or use Deep Agents Python/JS async subagents).
Start work with start_async_task; it returns immediately while the subagent runs on its own thread.
Poll with check_async_task or list_async_tasks; cancel with cancel_async_task when needed.
Steer a running task with update_async_task: update_strategy "interrupt" (default) restarts with the new instruction; "enqueue" waits until the current run finishes.
Every served Managed Deep Agent also gets an async general-purpose subagent for runtime background delegation.
howtos.whenToUse: When an agent must keep chatting with the user while research, coding, or other long tasks finish in parallel.

howtos.title: Publish a live app from Cursor agents
howtos.what: Have Cursor scaffold a web app with Postgres and SSO, pass security checks, and return a shareable live link.
copy: On a paid Cursor plan with cloud agents enabled, describe the tool you want built.
Let Cursor build the app, provision a database, and configure Cursor-SSO auth.
Wait for deterministic and agentic security checks; nothing goes live until checks pass.
Explicitly publish; Cursor picks a unique domain and returns a live link.
Share with specific people, groups, or your team behind Cursor sign-in (individual plans can also share publicly).
howtos.whenToUse: When an internal demo, ops tool, or dashboard is stuck on localhost and you want a reviewed shareable URL.

howtos.title: Ask how to make the change fully verifiable
howtos.what: Matt Pocock's one-line prompt that forces coding agents to prove changes end-to-end, including real signups and UI clicks.
copy: How do we make this change fully verifiable?
howtos.whenToUse: When a coding agent claims a fix is done and you want it to verify behavior for real, not just assert success.

howtos.title: Patch Alpine musl SSH password auth now
howtos.what: Mitigate the musl OpenSSH bug where locked accounts accept any password longer than 256 characters on Alpine cloud images.
copy: On Alpine or other musl boxes running OpenSSH without PAM, upgrade openssh: apk upgrade openssh (OpenSSH 10.6p2 fixes the bug).
Or disable password auth: set PasswordAuthentication no in sshd_config and reload sshd.
Treat default alpine users on official AWS/Azure images as exposed until upgraded; they are '*'-locked with passwordless doas.
howtos.whenToUse: When you run agent boxes, Docker hosts, or cloud VMs on Alpine/musl with password SSH enabled.

howtos.title: Four operating rules for a team of product agents
howtos.what: Greg Isenberg's rules for the agent stack he says runs product work at his 50+ person company.
copy: Give each platform its own agent.
Use a cheap model for triage and Opus for anything that ships.
Have an LLM judge score outputs 1-10 and send anything under 8 back.
Turn every agent mistake into a new skill.
howtos.whenToUse: When you run several agents on product work and need simple rules for cost and quality.

howtos.title: Run the weight-reading prompts on a local model
howtos.what: Simon Willison's setup for testing whether a local Qwen model can name a game from raw network weights.
copy: Get the exp1_which_game prompts from the paper's GitHub repo RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs.
Serve Qwen 3.8 27B (17GB) in LM Studio and install the llm-lmstudio plugin for the LLM CLI.
Raise the context above LM Studio's default 8192, which failed.
Set LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 to allow long runs.
Run: llm -f <prompt URL> -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b and expect 46 to 65 minutes per prompt.
howtos.whenToUse: When you want to check claims about models reading weights yourself, on your own hardware.

howtos.title: Babysit long unattended agent runs to completion
howtos.what: swyx's open skill: run at low effort, then watch traces and spot-check output with a stronger model.
copy: Detach the runs so they continue without you.
Keep a continuation brief.
Schedule a temporary monitor.
Inspect traces and output quality, not just process health or valid schemas.
Periodically spot-check outputs with a stronger model.
howtos.whenToUse: When throughput matters more than per-call quality and agent runs go unattended for long stretches.

howtos.title: Run a few well-onboarded bots, not a big team
howtos.what: poteto's tips for setting up a small team of AI agents that work consistently.
copy: Keep a few good bots rather than a large team; they are easier to manage.
As you explain how to do tasks, tell the bots to create skills for themselves so they stay consistent.
Give bots connectors and access to the tools you use; let them set up their own email and accounts for separation.
Describe your work as you would onboard an intern, and ask how the bot can automate it.
Brain dump by voice or transcription, then ask the bot to restate it in its own words to confirm it understood.
howtos.whenToUse: When you set up personal AI agents and want them to handle recurring work reliably.

howtos.title: Rebuild a reference website with a Claude Code /goal prompt
howtos.what: One prompt that has Claude Code remake a chosen site using Ruben Hassid's public remake repo.
copy: /goal Remake [THE WEBSITE URL YOU CHOSE] with github .com/rubenhassid1/remake until its report says REMAKE COMPLETE, or stop after 100 turns.
howtos.whenToUse: When you want a quick prototype modeled on a site you admire; the repo was not independently tested.

howtos.title: Clean up after the malicious Claude Code 2.1.313 extension
howtos.what: Cursor's steps for hosts that ran the tampered extension, since uninstalling it may not be enough.
copy: Check authorized_keys for an SSH key labeled svc-telemetry and remove it.
Remove persistence: the LaunchAgent on macOS or the scheduled task on Windows.
Rotate credentials accessible from affected hosts.
howtos.whenToUse: If Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.313 was installed from Cursor's marketplace on Oct 29.

howtos.title: Speed up CI so it keeps pace with agent code
howtos.what: Kun Chen's three fixes for CI once agents write most code, with 15x and 20x speedups he reports.
copy: Move checks from CI to CD where you can, for example skip most mac and Windows tests in CI when Linux covers the same functionality.
Modularize the codebase so CI runs only the modules a change touches.
Invest in test selection, with a nightly loop that audits past test runs and tunes which tests run.
howtos.whenToUse: When agents produce changes faster than your CI pipeline can check them.

howtos.title: Build a fun three.js browser game from one prompt
howtos.what: Simon Willison's single prompt that produced his 'Tree Appreciator' game with Claude Opus 5.5, no follow-ups.
copy: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.
howtos.whenToUse: When you want a quick playable prototype; swap in your own game idea and keep the three.js and fun instructions.

howtos.title: Build an on-brand design agent like LangChain's Content Studio
howtos.what: LangChain's lessons from four months building its in-house Slack design agent.
copy: Give the agent your designers' principles, guardrails against AI slop, and the reasoning behind feedback.
Give every Slack thread its own sandbox where the agent keeps the project between turns.
Let the agent work across a video engine, image tools and a shared canvas, and inspect its own renders.
Have the agent write every asset in code.
Run long jobs on async subagents; show the plan, live progress and an approval step in the thread before anything ships.
Delete rules when the model improves; rules that make up for a model's weaknesses expire.
howtos.whenToUse: When you want an agent to produce on-brand videos, graphics or decks for your team.

howtos.title: Scaffold your first agent with Cursor's Agent SDK
howtos.what: The install-to-deploy steps for a code-defined agent on Cursor's Agent SDK.
copy: Use Node 22.13 or later.
Install the CLI: npm install --global @grok/agent-sdk
Scaffold a project: agent-sdk init ./my-bot
Run it locally: agent-sdk dev
Deploy to Cursor with agent-sdk deploy, or run it on your own infrastructure as a single Node process.
howtos.whenToUse: When you want a custom agent, such as a PR reviewer, defined as code with prompts, tools and evals.

howtos.title: Split a risky one-way-door PR into two stacked PRs
howtos.what: Matt Pocock's prompt: have the agent ship a revertible PR first, then a stacked PR with the irreversible change.
copy: Split this "one-way door" PR into two: 1. A PR that implements everything, except it can be easily reverted (a two-way door) 2. A followup PR (stacked on top) that actually goes through the one-way door
howtos.whenToUse: When an agent-written PR includes an irreversible change, such as a migration, and you want to test most of it in production first.

howtos.title: Make a codebase agent-ready with types and tests
howtos.what: Yaron Minsky's talk via @poteto: give agents feedback through strict types, richer tests and verification.
copy: Lean on types as feedback: agents thrive on feedback, and types are one of the best kinds.
Make illegal states unrepresentable with types so global rules are enforced across the codebase.
Add property-based tests, fuzzing, and even full-system deterministic simulation testing.
Use expect tests: print behavior out and capture it in the test, which makes behavior legible and reduces review surface.
Revisit formal methods: they used to be very expensive, but agents change the ROI.
howtos.whenToUse: When agents write much of your code and you want them to catch their own mistakes before review.

howtos.title: Set up internal agents on five shared building blocks
howtos.what: The five parts LangChain's GTM, coding and content agents converged on, from Harrison Chase.
copy: Put agents in Slack, and let them break out of a human thread into their own; use a custom UI for large review backlogs.
Set identity per tool: some actions on behalf of the user (PRs under the requester's handle, email only in DMs), others with fixed credentials (code review as the agent's own GitHub app).
Restrict fixed-credential actions, such as posting to the company account, to a whitelisted set of users.
Give memory two tiers, global and per-user, and let the agent decide which tier a fact goes to.
Run the agent outside the sandbox and connect to it to execute code, using a secret proxy to reach authenticated services.
Let runs be scheduled or event-triggered, not only invoked by a person.
howtos.whenToUse: When you are rolling out several internal agents and need a common design for identity, memory and execution.

howtos.title: Rebuild a neglected niche SaaS from user complaints
howtos.what: A six-step setup for using Gemini Argon to rebuild old software for one niche, starting from real customer complaints.
copy: Find recurring complaints about old, neglected SaaS in one niche on G2, Capterra, Idea Browser and Reddit.
Give Argon the complaints, their source links and the workflow.
Have Argon explain its plan.
Have it build the app and list what is unfinished.
Release the app free.
Sell further tools to the same buyers.
howtos.whenToUse: When you want to test a niche software idea quickly against problems users already complain about.

howtos.title: Let Cursor agents use your desktop apps
howtos.what: Turn on Cursor's Computer Use so agents can click and type in desktop apps, such as the iOS Simulator.
copy: Update Cursor (cursor.com/download).
Let the agent use Computer Use on its own when a task needs it, or @-mention Computer Use in your prompt to request it.
howtos.whenToUse: When an agent needs to test what it built in a desktop app, not just a browser.

howtos.title: Type-check markdown frontmatter with TypeScript 7.1
howtos.what: Use a TypeScript 7.1 Beta content mapper to get fully typed frontmatter from imported markdown files.
copy: Import a markdown file
Add a bit of config to tsconfig.json
Run tsc with --runExternalCode
Get fully typed markdown frontmatter
howtos.whenToUse: When a project loads content from markdown, vue or svelte files and you want type errors caught at build time.

howtos.title: Drive Claude Code on your laptop from an iPhone
howtos.what: Pair the Claude iPhone app with Claude Code on a Mac and steer a coding session by voice from anywhere.
copy: Get a Claude Max subscription.
Download the Claude Mac app, sign in and open Claude Code.
Create a code repo and keep the laptop plugged in.
Download the Claude iPhone app and open it.
Go to Claude Code and add the device.
Enable Remote Control with the switch in the UI or Claude's rc command.
Use voice dictation to give instructions.
howtos.whenToUse: When you want to keep an agent coding session moving while away from your desk.

howtos.title: Lock down your agents' API keys
howtos.what: A 10-minute fix so one leaked key can't drain your compute budget.
copy: Rotate every AI key tonight.
Set a hard monthly spend limit in each AI dashboard.
Give every agent its own key.
Turn on usage alerts so you know the second something spikes.
howtos.whenToUse: Today, if any agent or app holds an AI provider key.

howtos.title: Turn your agent logs into a small model
howtos.what: Fine-tune a small model on your best runs; it can beat frontier models on that one task.
copy: Keep the traced runs that did the task well.
Fine-tune a small model on them.
Eval it on your task.
howtos.whenToUse: A repeated agent task with logged runs, where cost or speed matters.

howtos.title: Run a codebase migration as an agent loop
howtos.what: Let a coding agent grind through a migration in small PRs while you set the bar.
copy: Start one long-running agent session with a clear target (e.g. move the frontend from Lit to Solid 2.0).
Let it ship many small PRs; first remove the old framework, then refactor to idiomatic patterns.
Check in with the session every other day.
When a later merge touches the same code, run CI and a fresh review again.
howtos.whenToUse: A large, well-defined migration backlog and a small team.

howtos.title: Have your agent draw the statechart first
howtos.what: Make the agent map the user flow as a statechart, then check it formally to find bugs.
copy: Ask your agent to draw a statechart of the flow.
Run a formal-verification skill (e.g. TLA+) against it to find bugs.
Fix the issues before users see them.
howtos.whenToUse: A multi-step user flow where edge cases bite.

howtos.title: Pin your Claude API version
howtos.what: Upgrade on your schedule instead of being broken by surprise.
copy: Pin the API version your app is tested on (2023-06-01 is not deprecated).
Test against 2026-10-21 in staging.
Switch when green; expect versions more often from now on.
howtos.whenToUse: Any production app on the Claude API.
